subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Aerodynamics Revolution
description: A 60-second lesson on The Aerodynamics Revolution.

hook.text: In the 1960s, engineers realized that air flowing over a car could push it down instead of slow it.

buildup.text: Wings mounted upside down created downforce—pressing the tires harder into the track.

discovery.text: More downforce meant faster cornering, so cars could brake later and carry more speed through turns.

twist.text: Some early wings collapsed at speed, launching cars into catastrophic crashes before rules tightened.

climax.text: Today's F1 cars generate enough downforce to drive upside down on a ceiling at highway speed.

punchline.text: Pushing a car down lets it corner faster than gravity alone.

quiz.question: What do aerodynamic wings on race cars create?

details.summary: The discovery of aerodynamic downforce in the late 1960s transformed racing by allowing cars to corner at speeds previously impossible, using inverted wing shapes to push the car onto the track.
details.whyItMatters: Downforce changed the fundamental physics of racing. Cars could now corner faster than they accelerated, making aerodynamic design the most important performance differentiator in modern motorsport.
takeaways: Wings and ground effect create downforce pushing cars to the track
Modern F1 cars generate enough downforce to drive upside down
Aerodynamic development consumes the largest share of F1 team budgets

faq.question: How much downforce does a modern F1 car produce?
faq.answer: At high speed, an F1 car generates over 3.5 times its own weight in downforce. This is theoretically enough to drive on the ceiling of a tunnel, though no one has tested this in practice.

faq.question: Why was ground effect banned and then brought back in F1?
faq.answer: Ground effect was banned in the 1980s after cars suddenly lost all grip in accidents. F1 reintroduced it in 2022 with safer designs that allow cars to follow each other more closely, improving racing.
